cards.title: Understanding Dependency Injection (DI)
cards.content:
Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern used to achieve Inversion of Control (IoC). Instead of an object creating its own dependencies, the Spring IoC Container instantiates, configures, and injects them at runtime.

This promotes loose coupling, making applications modular and significantly easier to unit-test.

options.text: It speeds up compile-time performance of Java code.
It decouples classes, allowing easier testing and maintainability.
It replaces the need for database connections entirely.
It automatically deploys applications to cloud servers.

cards.title: Spring Stereotype Annotations
cards.content:
To tell Spring which classes it should manage as Beans, we use stereotype annotations:

  • @Component: Generic stereotype for any Spring-managed component.
  • @Service: Specializes @Component for business logic layers.
  • @Repository: Specializes @Component for data access layers (handles DB exceptions).
  • @Controller: Specializes @Component for presentation layers (Spring MVC).

pairs.right: Business logic and service orchestration layer
Data Access Object (DAO) and database operations
Web presentation tier handling HTTP requests
Generic Spring-managed utility bean or component

cards.title: Constructor vs Field Injection
cards.content:
There are three primary ways to inject dependencies:

  1. Constructor Injection: Best practice. Guarantees required dependencies are immutable and not null.
  2. Setter Injection: Useful for optional or mutable dependencies.
  3. Field Injection: Simplest syntax using @Autowired directly on fields, but highly discouraged due to testing limitations and tight coupling with Spring framework APIs.

Understanding Spring Bean Scopes
cards.content:
Spring Beans can have different lifecycles depending on their defined scope:

  • singleton: (Default) Only one instance per Spring IoC container.
  • prototype: A brand new instance is created every time the bean is requested.
  • request: One instance per single HTTP request.
  • session: One instance per HTTP session lifetime.

cards.title: Handling Ambiguity with Multiple Beans
cards.content:
When Spring finds multiple beans of the same type, it throws a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException.

We resolve this using two key annotations:

  • @Primary: Tells Spring to prioritize this bean over others of the same type.
  • @Qualifier("beanName"): Explicitly selects a specific bean by name at the injection point.

cards.title: Module Summary
cards.content:
You have successfully mastered Spring Boot Dependency Injection!

  • Always favor Constructor Injection over Field Injection.
  • Use Stereotypes like @Service and @Repository to define beans.
  • Leverage @Qualifier to manage multiple bean variations.
